\chapter{Numbers One to Ten}
\label{ch:te-numbers-one-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in Telugu, including the numbers that wander furthest from their Dravidian cousins.}

Count \te{ఒకటి} through \te{పది}, say the two Telugu builds fresh — enimidi and tommidi — and hear seven's three fates in ēḻu, ēḷu and ēḍu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[okaṭi reṇḍu mūḍu nālugu aidu]{\te{ఒకటి}, \te{రెండు}, \te{మూడు}, \te{నాలుగు}, \te{ఐదు} — one to five}

\label{lesson:TE-C07-numbers-1-5}



\begin{quote}
Four of these five are old Dravidian friends. The very first one is Telugu going its own way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The five}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{numeral} & \textbf{word} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
1 & \textbf{\te{౧}} & \textbf{\te{ఒకటి}} & \emph{okaṭi} \\
2 & \textbf{\te{౨}} & \textbf{\te{రెండు}} & \emph{reṇḍu} \\
3 & \textbf{\te{౩}} & \textbf{\te{మూడు}} & \emph{mūḍu} \\
4 & \textbf{\te{౪}} & \textbf{\te{నాలుగు}} & \emph{nālugu} \\
5 & \textbf{\te{౫}} & \textbf{\te{ఐదు}} & \emph{aidu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The symbols \textbf{\te{౧} \te{౨} \te{౩} \te{౪} \te{౫}} are Telugu's own digits.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{One} is where Telugu leaves the family. Its cousins agree — Tamil \emph{oṉṟu}, Kannada \emph{ondu}, Malayalam \emph{onnu}, all from an old \emph{oṉ-} — but Telugu says \textbf{okaṭi}, a different formation altogether. It's the number to memorise fresh rather than reason across from Tamil.

From two onward, the family closes ranks again:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{Telugu} \\
\midrule
2 & \emph{iraṇṭu} & \textbf{reṇḍu} \\
3 & \emph{mūṉṟu} & \textbf{mūḍu} \\
4 & \emph{nāṉku} & \textbf{nālugu} \\
5 & \emph{aintu} & \textbf{aidu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Reṇḍu} has simply dropped the opening vowel of \emph{iraṇṭu}; \emph{mūḍu} is \emph{mūṉṟu} with its cluster smoothed to a single \textbf{ḍ}. Same numbers, a Telugu polish.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: A Telugu shape to notice}
Nearly every Telugu word here ends in \textbf{‑u} (\emph{reṇḍu, mūḍu, nālugu}) — the language's strong preference for open, vowel-final syllables. Even where Tamil ends hard, Telugu tends to round the word off with a vowel.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}okaṭi, reṇḍu, mūḍu, nālugu, aidu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the maverick — \textquotedblleft{}okaṭi\textquotedblright{}, NOT the oṉṟu/ondu/onnu of its cousins
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}iraṇṭu $\to$ reṇḍu\textquotedblright{}, the opening vowel dropped
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to five in Telugu. (\emph{Okaṭi, reṇḍu, mūḍu, nālugu, aidu}.) Which number does Telugu form unlike the rest of the family, and what do the others say? (\textbf{One} — Telugu \emph{okaṭi} vs \emph{oṉṟu / ondu / onnu}.) How does \emph{reṇḍu} relate to Tamil \emph{iraṇṭu}? (The opening vowel was dropped.) What vowel do most Telugu words here end in? (\textbf{‑u}.) Next: six to ten.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\te{ఐ} — one letter for a vowel that moves}

\label{lesson:TE-S164-letter-ai}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ఏ} — what sound, and where in a word does Telugu use the letter rather than the sign?

Count to five out loud. The last number opens on today's character.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ఐ}}
\textbf{\te{ఐ}} — \emph{ai}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — a vowel that is a letter in its own right, not a mark hung on a consonant.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ఐదు}} \emph{aidu} — five
\end{itemize}

Say \emph{aidu} slowly and listen to the opening. Your mouth does not hold one position: it starts low and slides up toward \emph{i}. Two sounds in one movement, which is what the romanization's two letters are trying to show.

\textbf{Telugu writes that whole movement with one character.} English needs a digraph or a silent letter for the same job — \emph{aisle}, \emph{height}, \emph{my} — and picks a different trick each time. Here the slide has a shape of its own, and it looks nothing like the \te{ఏ} you met a chapter ago even though the romanizations share a letter.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ఐ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ఐ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed. Then write \te{ఏ} beside it and look at the two.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the number below and find \te{ఐ} at its front
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ఐదు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ఐ} three times, saying \emph{ai} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēmiṭi} and \emph{aidu} one after the other, and say which opening moves
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ఐ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ai}}.) Which number begins with it? (\textbf{\te{ఐదు}}.) Does your mouth hold one position for it or two? (\textbf{Two} — it slides.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\te{◌ూ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S134-vowel-sign-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{య} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{హ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ూ}}
\textbf{\te{◌ూ}} — \emph{ū}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already know its short partner. \textbf{\te{◌ు}} puts a quick \emph{u} on a consonant; \textbf{\te{◌ూ}} puts a \textbf{held} one on it — the same vowel, kept twice as long. Telugu counts that length as the difference between two different words, so the two signs are two different characters and not two ways of writing one.

Say \emph{mu}, then say \emph{mū} and let the vowel run on. That extra length is all the second mark is asking for.

You already say this one, and the held vowel is sitting in the middle of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{మూడు}} \emph{mūḍu} — three, from the numbers you counted out
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ూ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ూ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one holds its vowel and which one does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{మూడు}  ·  \te{రెండు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ూ} three times, saying \emph{ū} and holding it as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ూ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ూ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to, and how is it different from \te{◌ు}? (\textbf{A held \emph{ū}; \te{◌ు} is the short one.})

One more, from much earlier: \te{౫} — what amount does it stand for?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āru ēḍu enimidi tommidi padi]{\te{ఆరు}, \te{ఏడు}, \te{ఎనిమిది}, \te{తొమ్మిది}, \te{పది} — six to ten}

\label{lesson:TE-C07-numbers-6-10}



\begin{quote}
The top of the count is where Telugu is least like its cousins — two of these you simply learn on their own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The five}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{numeral} & \textbf{word} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
6 & \textbf{\te{౬}} & \textbf{\te{ఆరు}} & \emph{āru} \\
7 & \textbf{\te{౭}} & \textbf{\te{ఏడు}} & \emph{ēḍu} \\
8 & \textbf{\te{౮}} & \textbf{\te{ఎనిమిది}} & \emph{enimidi} \\
9 & \textbf{\te{౯}} & \textbf{\te{తొమ్మిది}} & \emph{tommidi} \\
10 & \textbf{\te{౧౦}} & \textbf{\te{పది}} & \emph{padi} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{cousinweb}
Six is an easy cousin (Tamil \emph{āṟu} $\to$ Telugu \emph{āru}). \textbf{Seven} is more interesting: Tamil \emph{ēḻu} carries the rare \textbf{ḻ} (the \emph{zh} of \emph{Tamiḻ}); Kannada hardened it to \textbf{ḷ} (\emph{ēḷu}); \textbf{Telugu went further still} and turned it into a plain \textbf{ḍ} — \emph{ēḍu}. One inherited sound, three fates across the three scripts.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here Telugu strays furthest from its cousins —

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{Malayalam} & \textbf{Telugu} \\
\midrule
8 & \emph{eṭṭu} & \emph{eṭṭu} & \textbf{enimidi} \\
9 & \emph{oṉpatu} & \emph{onpatu} & \textbf{tommidi} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You can't reach \emph{enimidi} and \emph{tommidi} from Tamil by regular sound-change the way you can \emph{reṇḍu} from \emph{iraṇṭu}: \emph{tommidi} is a different word entirely, and \emph{enimidi} — though it shares the ancient \emph{eṇ-} root behind \emph{eṭṭu} — has drifted too far to derive. So unlike 2–7, learn these two \textbf{fresh}.

\textbf{Ten} comes partly back into the fold — Telugu \emph{padi} is a worn-down relative of the \emph{pat‑} in Tamil \emph{pattu} (and the \emph{‑patu} hiding inside \emph{tommidi} and Tamil \emph{oṉpatu}, \textquotedblleft{}one-to-ten\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āru, ēḍu, enimidi, tommidi, padi\textquotedblright{}
  \item seven's three fates — \textquotedblleft{}Tamil ēḻu, Kannada ēḷu, Telugu ēḍu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two you learn fresh — \textquotedblleft{}enimidi, tommidi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count six to ten in Telugu. (\emph{Āru, ēḍu, enimidi, tommidi, padi}.) What became of Tamil's \textbf{ḻ} (in \emph{ēḻu}) by the time it reached Telugu \emph{ēḍu}? (It hardened all the way to \textbf{ḍ}.) Which two numbers can't you derive from Tamil by regular correspondence? (\textbf{Eight and nine} — learn \emph{enimidi, tommidi} fresh.) How does \emph{padi} relate to Tamil \emph{pattu}? (A worn-down relative of the same \emph{pat‑} \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\te{ొ} — the short one of the pair}

\label{lesson:TE-S154-vowel-sign-o}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ూ} — is it a letter or a sign, and what does it do?

Count from six to ten out loud. One of those numbers needs today's sign.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ొ}}
\textbf{\te{ొ}} — \emph{o}.

It is a \textbf{sign}, like the long \textbf{\te{ో}} you have already met, and it carries the \textbf{short} \emph{o} where that one carries the long \emph{ō}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{తొమ్మిది}} \emph{tommidi} — nine (tommidi)
\end{itemize}

Telugu keeps short and long vowels apart as separate signs, and the difference changes words. English writes one \emph{o} and leaves the length to the ear; here the page tells you, which is one less thing to guess at.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ొ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ొ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed. Then write it attached to a consonant, the way it actually appears.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the number below and find the consonant carrying \te{ొ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{తొమ్మిది}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ొ} three times, saying \emph{o} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \te{ొ} and \te{ో} is the long one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \te{సంతోషం} and find the long one riding its consonant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \te{ొ} a letter or a sign? (A sign.) Which number from this chapter uses it? (\textbf{\te{తొమ్మిది}}, nine.) Which of the two \emph{o} signs is longer? (\textbf{\te{ో}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\te{ఒ} — the sign from a page ago, standing alone}

\label{lesson:TE-S165-letter-o}



\begin{quote}
A page ago you met \te{◌ొ}, the short-\emph{o} sign, inside \te{తొమ్మిది}. Say that number.

Now count from one. The first number opens on the same vowel, and it has no consonant to hang the sign on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ఒ}}
\textbf{\te{ఒ}} — \emph{o}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — a vowel that is a letter in its own right, not a mark hung on a consonant.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ఒకటి}} \emph{okaṭi} — one
\end{itemize}

This is the clearest pair you will get. \textbf{\te{◌ొ}} and \textbf{\te{ఒ}} are the same vowel: the first rides on a consonant, the second stands where no consonant does. You met the sign one lesson ago inside \emph{tommidi}; here is the letter, at the front of \emph{okaṭi}, in the same chapter and the same list of numbers.

Hold the two next to each other and the whole system is visible in one line:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the vowel is carried} & \textbf{the vowel starts the word} \\
\midrule
\te{తొమ్మిది} — the sign \te{◌ొ} rides on \te{త} & \te{ఒకటి} — the letter \te{ఒ} stands alone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ఒ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ఒ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed. Then write \te{◌ొ} beside it and look at the two.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two numbers and say which one carries the letter \te{ఒ} and which the sign \te{◌ొ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ఒకటి}  ·  \te{తొమ్మిది}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ఒ} three times, saying \emph{o} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} the numbers one to five, and name the one that opens on a vowel letter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ఒ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{o}}.) Which number begins with it? (\textbf{\te{ఒకటి}}.) And what is the difference between \te{ఒ} and \te{◌ొ}? (\textbf{None in the sound} — one stands alone, the other rides on a consonant.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\te{ఆ} — the long one, beside the short one that needs no sign}

\label{lesson:TE-S166-letter-aa}



\begin{quote}
Two from the first chapter: \te{అ}, and the sign \te{◌ా}. Say what each of them does.

Today's character is the missing corner of that square.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ఆ}}
\textbf{\te{ఆ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — a vowel that is a letter in its own right, not a mark hung on a consonant.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ఆరు}} \emph{āru} — six
\end{itemize}

With this one the \emph{a} vowels are complete, and they make a square worth drawing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{short} & \textbf{long} \\
\midrule
\textbf{carried by a consonant} & nothing at all & \te{◌ా} \\
\textbf{starting a word} & \te{అ} & \te{ఆ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of those four cells you have had since chapter one. \textbf{The top-left cell is the one that surprises people}: short \emph{a} on a consonant is written with no mark, which is why \te{క} is \emph{ka} and not \emph{k}. Every other cell gets a shape.

Look at the two letters side by side — \te{అ} and \te{ఆ}. The long one is the short one with a stroke added on the right, and that stroke has the same shape as the sign \te{◌ా}. Length shows up on the page as \emph{more ink}, in both columns of the square.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ఆ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ఆ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed. Then write \te{అ} beside it and find the difference.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and say which opens on \te{అ} and which on \te{ఆ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{అవును}  ·  \te{ఆరు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ఆ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{avunu} and \emph{āru}, holding the opening vowel of the second one longer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ఆ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ā}}.) Which number begins with it? (\textbf{\te{ఆరు}}.) Which cell of the square has no shape in it at all? (\textbf{Short \emph{a} carried by a consonant} — the consonant alone says it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(dialogue)]{The name exchange again — built from four pieces}

\label{lesson:TE-C07-second-pass-names}



\begin{quote}
Two words, from memory: the one for \emph{name}, and the one for \emph{my}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: four pieces, and everything they build}
The question you learned and its answer are made of the same four pieces:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{పేరు}} \emph{pēru} & name \\
\textbf{\te{నా}} \emph{nā} · \textbf{\te{మీ}} \emph{mī} & my · your \\
\textbf{\te{ఏమిటి}} \emph{ēmiṭi} & what? \\
\textbf{\te{నువ్వు}} \emph{nuvvu} · \textbf{\te{మీరు}} \emph{mīru} & you, close · you, respectful \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two side by side give the answer, \textbf{\te{నా} \te{పేరు} …} The respectful one in front and the question word behind give the question, \textbf{\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two things the name exchange was really teaching}]
Two points sit under those four pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{No word for \emph{is}.} \emph{Nā pēru Arun} is \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun,\textquotedblright{} and the link stays unsaid in every sentence of this shape.
  \item \textbf{Respect rides on the plural.} \textbf{\te{మీరు}} is a plural doing the work of politeness — the move Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ} and French \emph{vous} also make.
\end{itemize}

The familiar \emph{your} goes with the familiar \emph{you}: \textbf{\te{నీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Script: three letters that open numbers}
\begin{quote}
\te{ఒ} · \te{ఐ} · \te{ఆ}
\end{quote}

Three vowel letters come back with the counting. Each opens a number you now say, and each is a whole letter rather than a sign for one reason: nothing is carrying the vowel.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{the number it opens} \\
\midrule
\te{ఒ} \emph{o} & \te{ఒకటి} — one \\
\te{ఐ} \emph{ai} & \te{ఐదు} — five \\
\te{ఆ} \emph{ā} & \te{ఆరు} — six \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Your turn: the exchange, both ways}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ask a stranger their name, then answer with your own — no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one word for \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same question to a child — one letter of \emph{mī} changes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word does \textbf{\te{నా} \te{పేరు} …} leave out? (\textbf{Is}.) Which \emph{you} goes to a stranger, and what is it really? (\textbf{\te{మీరు}} — a plural doing politeness.) One word for \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\te{సంతోషం}}.) Which three numbers open on a whole vowel letter? (\textbf{\te{ఒకటి} · \te{ఐదు} · \te{ఆరు}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
